transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in today. What brings you in?

Well, I came in because, honestly, my husband and the people at the warehouse—they all just keep acting like I'm crazy. Like I'm making things up or something. But I'm not. I know what I see, and I know what's going on. They have been watching my every move at work. Every single thing I do. I mean, I'm just a material mover, right? I move the pallets, I do the heavy lifting, I mind my own business. But I started noticing little things, you know? Like, the way they look at me when I walk past the breakroom, or how the shift manager is always suddenly right there when I'm loading the freight. And it’s not just watching me, either. They are actually going in and changing the pallet counts on my logs. I know they are. I count them, I write it down, and then later, the numbers are different. And I know exactly why they’re doing it, too. It’s because they want to keep me from getting that supervisor spot that opened up. They know I work hard, they know I deserve it, so they have to try and make me look bad, make me look like I can't keep track of my own freight. And my husband, he just rolls his eyes and tells me I need to calm down, that I'm overthinking it, but he doesn't work there. He doesn't see how they are constantly monitoring me and messing with my work just to keep me down. So, yeah, that's why I'm here. Because everyone thinks I'm losing it, but I'm the only one actually paying attention to what they're doing to me.
Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?

Well, I mean... it's not like I'm hearing ghosts or, you know, a whole crowd of people or anything crazy like that. But, yeah, sometimes... sometimes I do hear something. It's usually when I'm just working, like when I'm down one of the long aisles at the warehouse, just trying to get the pallets lined up right. Or even when I'm at home, just doing something completely normal, like folding the laundry in the bedroom. I'll be standing there, just matching up socks or whatever, and I'll hear this man's voice. And it is clear as day. It’s not a mumble, it’s not the wind, it’s a real voice. And he always says the exact same thing. He says, "Nicole, check it again." Just like that. And the first time it happened at work, I spun right around, thinking it was the shift manager sneaking up on me again, trying to catch me making a mistake with the freight logs. Because, like I said, they are always messing with my numbers. But there was nobody there. The aisle was completely empty. And then it happened at home, and I thought maybe my husband had come into the room, but he was all the way out in the garage. So, I don't know who it is, but it's a man, and he wants me to keep checking things, which makes sense because I have to be so careful with my counts so they don't ruin my chances at that supervisor job. But yeah, nobody is ever near me when he says it.
Have you had a period where you felt unusually high or energized for days at a time?

Well, yeah, actually. I mean, it's not like I'm running around the block a hundred times or anything, but there are these days—like, stretches of days—where I just feel completely fired up. It's like I have this electricity buzzing right under my skin, and nobody can slow me down. I’ll go into the warehouse, and I’m just moving pallets left and right, getting everything done faster than anyone else on the floor. I feel like I could work a double shift and still come home and clean the entire house top to bottom. And I feel good, you know? Like I’m finally on top of things, like I’m unstoppable. But then, the flip side of it is that I get so... I don't even know the right word. Just on edge, I guess. Because I’ll be in this groove, feeling like I can take on the world, and then my husband will come in and just ruin it. He’ll ask me one small, stupid question, like, "Hey, did you remember to pick up the kids' permission slips?" or "What time are you working tomorrow?" And it’s like a switch flips in my brain. I just snap at him. I mean, I completely go off. And it’s because it feels like he’s trying to control me, you know? Like he’s trying to throw a wrench in my gears right when I’m moving at top speed. He’ll look at me like I’m a monster, but he doesn't understand that when I'm feeling that energized, I don't have time for his little interruptions. I have things to do, big things, and him just standing there asking about a schedule... it just makes me so mad I can hardly see straight. So, yeah, I get really, really energized, but it also makes me just want to bite someone's head off if they get in my way.
During those fired-up stretches, do you need less sleep than usual?

Oh, definitely. It's actually kind of crazy when I think about it, because normally I'm someone who needs a solid night of sleep, especially with all the heavy lifting and pulling I do at the warehouse. You can't just be half-asleep when you're moving heavy freight, you know? But when I get into one of those stretches where I'm all fired up... I mean, there have been entire weeks where I sleep maybe three hours a night. Tops. 

I'll go to bed at like, I don't know, midnight or one in the morning, mostly just because my husband is complaining about the lights being on, but my mind is still just going and going, thinking about the pallet counts and figuring out how to prove the shift manager is messing with my logs. And then, boom. It's 3:30 or 4:00 AM, and my eyes just snap open. Way before my alarm is even set to go off. I have it set for 5:30, but I never even hear it during those weeks because I'm already up. 

And the weirdest part is, you'd think I'd be dragging, right? Like, running on empty. But I'm not. I wake up before the alarm, and I feel like I don't need any more rest to get moving. I'm just instantly wide awake, completely recharged, and ready to go. I'll just get out of bed and start doing things. I'll organize the kitchen cabinets, or I'll scrub the baseboards, or I'll sit at the table going over my work notes with a fine-tooth comb. And my husband will wake up and come out to the kitchen, rubbing his eyes, and he'll be like, "What are you doing, it's pitch black outside?" and I just look at him like he's the one who's crazy. Because I'm getting things done, obviously. I just don't need the sleep. My body just runs on that electricity I was talking about. I don't need to lie there in the dark wasting time when I could be preparing for the day, making sure I'm sharp and ready for whatever they try to pull on me at work.
Have the voice and the feeling that people at work are watching or sabotaging you ever happened when you were not in one of those fired-up periods?

Yeah, actually, they have. It’s not just when I’m running on three hours of sleep and buzzing around the warehouse, you know? Like, there was this one time, maybe a couple of months ago, where I had a really quiet stretch. It was a few weeks where I was actually sleeping through the night, mostly. I mean, I was still waking up maybe once to get a glass of water, but I was getting my solid seven or eight hours, going to bed at a normal time, and I wasn't feeling that electric charge under my skin. I was just... steady, I guess you could say. Not racing around, not snapping at my husband for breathing too loud. Just going to work, doing my job, coming home, making dinner. A completely normal routine.

But even then, even when I felt totally fine and grounded, I was still hearing him. I’d be in the aisle, moving a pallet of dog food or something, and I’d hear, "Nicole, check it again." Clear as day, just like always. And I still knew, without a shadow of a doubt, that the shift manager was messing with my numbers. I mean, I’d look at the freight logs, and I could just tell they’d been altered. The counts wouldn't match what I knew I’d loaded, and I knew they were doing it to keep me from getting that supervisor spot. It didn't matter that I wasn't all fired up or full of energy—I still had to double-check everything because the sabotage was still happening, and that voice was still warning me about it. So, yeah, it doesn't just go away when I'm sleeping better. It's always there, waiting for me to slip up so they can use it against me.
Have you ever had a period lasting at least two weeks when you felt depressed most of the day nearly every day?

No, not really. I mean, I don't think so. Like, depressed? Two straight weeks of just feeling down all day? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, sure, I have days where I'm tired or frustrated, especially when I know my manager is messing with my logs, you know? Like, that really gets to me. It makes me angry, mostly, but sometimes it just makes me feel like, what's the point of even trying so hard if they're just going to change the numbers anyway? So I guess I get frustrated, maybe a little bummed out about that specific thing, but it's not like I'm sitting around crying or unable to get out of bed for weeks on end. 

Even when I'm not in one of those fired-up periods, I'm still going to work. I have to. The warehouse doesn't stop just because I'm having a slow day. And my husband, he's always on me about paying the bills and keeping things running, so it's not like I have the luxury of just being depressed for two weeks. I just keep moving. I might not be scrubbing the baseboards at 4:00 AM, but I'm still getting up, packing my lunch, getting my boots on, and going in to move those pallets. So, no, I haven't had a time where I felt depressed like that, all day, every day, for weeks. I just don't have the time for it, honestly. I'm too busy trying to keep track of what's going on at work and making sure I don't miss anything important.
For at least one month, have you been hearing that man's voice or feeling sure that people at work were sabotaging you?

Oh, definitely. It's been way longer than a month. I mean, if I really sit down and trace it back to when I first started noticing the numbers being off and when that voice first started telling me to check things... it’s been about eight months now. Eight solid months of this. I remember because it started right around the time they brought in that new scanning system at the warehouse, which was supposed to make everything faster, but I knew right away it was just a way for them to track us closer and mess with the logs without us catching on as easily. 

And that voice, you know, "Nicole, check it again," it started right around then, too. At first, I thought maybe I was just stressing over the new system, but then I started seeing the discrepancies with my own eyes. So for eight months, every single day, whether I'm sleeping three hours or eight hours, whether I'm buzzing with energy or just doing my regular routine, I'm hearing him, and I'm having to constantly watch my back. Eight months of double-checking pallets, re-reading freight logs, and making sure my husband doesn't accidentally throw away any of the notes I bring home from my shifts. It’s a full-time job just keeping track of the sabotage on top of my actual full-time job moving the freight, you know? So, yes, way longer than a month. Eight months of it, at least.

Was there ever a time when you were hearing that man's voice or felt sure people at work were sabotaging you for at least two weeks while your mood was completely normal—not especially energized or irritable?

Yeah, I mean, I think I mentioned that earlier, right? Like, there was that stretch a couple of months ago where things were just... quiet. I wasn't buzzing, I wasn't staying up all night scrubbing the floors or getting into arguments with my husband over every little thing. I was actually getting my seven or eight hours of sleep, which is pretty rare for me, honestly. I’d go to bed around ten, wake up at six, make my coffee, pack my lunch—just a completely normal, boring routine. I wasn't feeling that electricity in my veins, you know? I was just steady. 

But even then, even during those few weeks when I was feeling totally grounded and not racing around the warehouse like a maniac, it didn't stop. I'd be out there, moving a pallet of dog food or stacking boxes of windshield wiper fluid, and clear as day, I'd hear him. "Nicole, check it again." Just like always. And I still knew, I mean, I was absolutely certain that the shift manager was messing with my numbers. I’d look at the freight logs, and I could see the discrepancies. The pallet counts wouldn't match what I knew I’d loaded. It didn't matter that my mood was completely normal and I wasn't all fired up. The sabotage was still happening, and the voice was still warning me about it. So, yeah, even when I was sleeping fine and feeling completely normal, for a solid few weeks there, I was still dealing with all of it. It's like it never takes a break, even when the rest of my brain decides to slow down for a minute.
What is the longest time those fired-up periods have lasted without stopping?

Oh, you mean like the longest one of those periods where I'm just going and going? Gosh, let me think about that. It's hard to pin down an exact number of days because when you're in it, time just kind of blurs together, you know? Like, you're not really looking at the calendar and marking off days when you're busy reorganizing the garage at 3:00 AM or trying to get the warehouse manager to listen to you about the logs. 

I guess... well, I don't really have a specific number for you. It's not like I keep a journal of every single day I feel fired up. I'm just too busy. I mean, my husband might know, he's the one who always complains about me keeping him awake or talking too fast, but if you're asking me for the absolute longest stretch? I'm honestly not sure. Sometimes it feels like it lasts for a good while, maybe a few weeks, where I'm just buzzing and getting everything done, and other times it feels shorter, but I couldn't tell you the record, so to speak. I just know it happens and then eventually I kind of crash back to normal, but I've never really timed it from start to finish.
Have any of those fired-up periods lasted at least one full week?

Oh, definitely a full week. Honestly, it's usually longer than that when I get into one of those grooves. Like, I’ll wake up on a Monday and just feel this—this surge, you know? Like I'm completely fired up and nobody can slow me down, not even the shift manager at the warehouse when he tries to tell me to pace myself. I'll be moving pallets twice as fast, getting everything sorted, coming home, scrubbing the baseboards, fixing the hinges on the cabinets, and it just keeps going like that for days and days, definitely a week or more. 

But the thing is, while I've got all this energy and I feel like I'm on top of the world, it can turn so fast. Like, I'll be right in the middle of getting things done, feeling great, and then my husband will come in and ask me one small, stupid question. Like, "Hey Nicole, what time are you picking up the kids?" or "Did you check your schedule for tomorrow?" And I just—I snap. I completely lose it on him. It feels like he's trying to control me or slow me down when I'm finally operating at my best. I'll start yelling, telling him to back off and let me handle my own life, and then we're in this huge fight over nothing. So yeah, I'll have that fired-up, unstoppable feeling for a solid week or more, but it comes with this edge where if anyone gets in my way or questions me, I just explode.
During those fired-up periods, do you feel more powerful, important, or capable than usual?

Powerful? I mean... not really? Like, what do you mean by powerful? Like a superhero or something? Because no, definitely not that. I don't think I'm, you know, the CEO of the company or anything crazy like that. I know who I am. I'm just Nicole, I didn't even finish high school—I dropped out in the eleventh grade, which my mom still gives me grief about sometimes, but whatever, I make decent money at the warehouse. So no, I don't walk around thinking I'm some big important VIP. 

The shift manager sure doesn't treat me like I'm important, that's for sure. Even when I'm in one of those grooves and I'm doing the work of three guys, moving those pallets of dog food faster than anyone else on the floor, he still talks down to me. So I definitely don't feel important. As for capable... I mean, I guess I feel capable of getting my chores done? Like I said, I can scrub the baseboards and fix the cabinet hinges and reorganize the whole garage all in one night. But it's not like I feel like I have special powers or I'm better than everyone else. I just feel awake. Really, really awake. 

And maybe a little annoyed that nobody else can keep up with me, honestly. My husband says I act like I'm the boss of the house when I get like that, but I'm not trying to be powerful, I'm just trying to get him to help me or at least get out of my way while I'm being productive. It's not about being in charge, it's just about getting things done because I finally have the energy to do them all at once. So, no, I wouldn't use those words. I just feel like a much faster version of myself, not somebody famous or important.
During those fired-up periods, do you talk much more than usual?

Talk more? I mean... no, not really. I don't think I talk any more than I usually do. Like I mentioned earlier, my husband will complain that I'm talking too fast, but that's not the same thing as talking *more*, you know? It's just that when I'm getting all those things done and I'm fired up, my brain is moving at a really good pace, so the words just come out quicker. But I'm not just standing around babbling about nothing. 

If I'm talking, it's because I have something specific to say, like when I'm trying to explain to him why the winter coats need to be moved away from the gardening tools in the garage because of the dampness, and he just stares at me like I'm speaking Greek. I'm just trying to communicate the plan so we can get it done, but he acts like I'm giving some massive lecture. I just want him to understand the system I'm setting up. 

And at work? I probably talk way less, honestly. When I'm in the zone moving freight, I'm completely focused. The warehouse is so loud anyway with the forklift backup alarms and the shift manager yelling over the radio, there's really no point in trying to have a conversation on the floor. I'm just focused on my pallets. I might yell if somebody gets in my way, sure, like I told you before, but I'm not chatting people's ears off by the breakroom coffee pot. So, no, I wouldn't say I talk more. I think people just don't listen fast enough when I do need to tell them something, which just makes me have to repeat myself, and maybe *that's* why my husband thinks I'm talking a lot. But it's definitely not like I'm just talking to hear my own voice.
During those fired-up periods, do you take on a lot more projects or activities than you usually would?

Oh, definitely. That is exactly what happens. It is like I just can't sit still, I have to be doing something, but not just one thing, I need to be doing like ten things at once. Like at the warehouse, I told you about my shift manager, right? Well, when I get in one of those grooves, I start thinking, why am I just moving pallets when I can run this place? So I started pushing really, really hard for a supervisor job. I was constantly going up to the front office, dropping off these lists of ideas I had for how to reorganize the loading docks, telling the boss I could handle the scheduling way better than the guys doing it now. They kept saying there were no openings, but I just kept pushing and pushing because I knew I could do it better and I wanted the extra responsibility. 

And it wasn't just at work, it was everywhere. Like at my church, I usually just sit in the back and head out right after the service. But during those times, I was signing up for every extra church task on the bulletin board. I volunteered to organize the whole food pantry drive, I told the pastor I would help repaint the Sunday school rooms, I even signed up to coordinate the spring potluck. Which is a huge headache normally, but I felt like I could do it all in my sleep. I just kept writing my name down on every clipboard they passed around. 

Then I would come home and I would be on my phone non-stop, just calling people about plans. Calling my cousin to see if we could meet up halfway for a weekend trip, calling girls I used to work with to set up these big dinners, just calling and calling because I had all this drive to do things and be out doing stuff. 

Oh, and the boxing. I have always liked messing around with the heavy bag in the garage, but I started trying
Have you been hearing that man's voice or feeling sure people at work were sabotaging you for at least six months in total?

Six months? Oh, it's been longer than that. Yeah, definitely longer. I'd say... well, it's been about eight months now. Eight whole months of dealing with this. I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time the weather started getting really cold, like late October, early November maybe? I was out in the garage, trying to fix the latch on the side door because the wind kept blowing it open, and that's the first time I heard him. Just this low, steady voice, right over my shoulder, telling me I was doing it wrong. I whipped around, and of course, nobody was there. Just me and the rakes. And ever since then, he just... he doesn't leave. Sometimes he's quiet for a bit, but he always comes back.

And the stuff at work, the sabotaging... that started right around the same time. Eight months of walking into the warehouse and just knowing, absolutely knowing, that they were messing with my pallets. I'd leave a stack perfectly shrink-wrapped, perfectly aligned, and I'd come back from my fifteen-minute break, and it would be slightly off. Just a fraction of an inch, but I could tell. I have an eye for that kind of thing. And they'd look at me, the shift manager and the other guys, they'd look at me with these little smirks, pretending they didn't do anything. But I know they did. They were moving things, changing the manifests, trying to make me look crazy or incompetent so I wouldn't get that supervisor job. So yeah, the voice, the feeling of being watched, the pallets being messed with... it's been a solid eight months of this, every single day, just wearing me down. It's exhausting, honestly, having to be on guard for eight straight months like that.
Have there been at least four straight weeks when you were hearing the man's voice or felt sure people were sabotaging you while your mood was completely normal?

Yeah, actually, there was a stretch exactly like that. Let me think... it was maybe a couple of months ago? I remember it clearly because my husband even made a comment about it. He was like, "Wow, it's nice you're actually sitting down to watch a movie with me," because usually, like I said, I'm up and down, pacing, fixing the weather stripping, making lists. But for like a solid month, maybe even five weeks, I was just... regular. I was having a really quiet few weeks. I was sleeping a good seven or eight hours a night, which is a huge deal for me, and I wasn't racing around trying to run the whole warehouse or signing up for a million church things. I was just clocking in, doing my job, coming home, eating dinner. Just a totally normal routine. 

But the thing is, even though I was feeling totally fine and my mood was completely calm, that guy's voice did not stop. Not even for a day. I’d be sitting there on the couch, drinking a soda, completely relaxed, and he’d be right there muttering at me, telling me I needed to go check things. Check the locks, check the garage, check my pallet stacks. It was constant. 

And the sabotage at work didn't stop either. I'd go in, feeling totally level, not fired up or arguing with anyone, but I still absolutely knew they were messing with my numbers. I'd look at the manifest and I could see that the pallet counts were being changed against me. Like, I’d wrap 42 pallets of freight, I'd count them twice, and then the shift sheet would suddenly say 40. I knew it was them
During one of those fired-up periods, were you ever hospitalized because of it?

Hospitalized? No, no, I've never been in the hospital for any of this. I mean, I know sometimes people get so worked up they end up in the ER or something, but that hasn't happened to me. Even when I was pushing so hard for that supervisor job, and going up to the front office every single day with my lists, and calling everyone I knew, I was still, you know, functioning. I was still going to work, I was still showing up at church, I was still doing all the things I signed up for. It's not like I crashed my car or stopped eating or anything that would make someone call an ambulance. 

I mean, my husband, he definitely gets annoyed with me when I'm like that. He'll tell me to sit down, tell me I'm wearing him out just watching me. He says I talk too fast and I don't let him get a word in edgewise. And I guess I do get pretty intense, like with the boxing in the garage, I was out there at 3 AM hitting the bag so hard I thought the chain was going to snap. But even then, I wasn't hurting myself or anyone else. I was just... full of energy, you know? Just overflowing with it. So, no, no hospitals. I've always managed to ride it out at home, even if it drives everyone around me a little crazy while it's happening. I just keep moving until it finally starts to fade out on its own.
During those fired-up periods, did the voice or your beliefs about sabotage ever get noticeably stronger than usual?

Oh, absolutely. It all kind of... feeds into each other, you know? Like, when I'm in one of those really high-gear phases, when I'm barely sleeping, maybe getting two, three hours a night if I'm lucky, and I'm pushing for all those extra shifts at the warehouse, plus the 3 AM boxing sessions in the garage, plus organizing the bake sale and the clothing drive for the church all at the exact same time... that's when everything else gets dialed up to an eleven, too. 

It's like my brain is moving a million miles an hour, and the voice... the man's voice gets louder, more insistent. He doesn't just mutter when I'm fired up like that; he practically shouts. He'll be telling me I'm missing things, that I need to work faster, that I need to check the manifests again, check them three times, four times. And the sabotage stuff... oh man. When I'm running on that kind of energy, I am just so hyper-aware of everything. Every single look the shift manager gives me, every time someone walks past my pallets, I just know, I am absolutely certain they are plotting against me. I can see the whole setup so clearly. I'll be flying around the warehouse on a forklift, trying to do the work of three people to prove I deserve that supervisor spot, and I'll just feel it in my bones that they're actively trying to trip me up, changing the numbers on the clipboard the second I turn my back. So yeah, when I'm all revved up and doing a hundred things at once, the voice and the feeling that I'm being set up are right there with me, running just as fast and just as hard as I am. It's like they feed off the energy, if that makes sense.
During those fired-up periods, did your behavior ever cause serious problems at work, at home, or with other people?

Well, yeah, I guess you could say it caused some problems. I mean, at work, it definitely did. It's actually really frustrating to think about, to be honest. See, when I was trying so hard to get that supervisor spot, and I was just buzzing with all that energy, I was checking things constantly. I mean, I had to, right? Because of the voice telling me to check, and because I knew they were messing with my numbers. So I'd be on the forklift, and I'd stop to recount a pallet, or I'd go back over my whole manifest three or four times, just to be absolutely sure everything was perfect. But my supervisors... they didn't see it that way. They pulled me into the office, and they were like, "You're slowing down the line, you're holding up the trucks," all this stuff. And then they actually took me off the forklift entirely. Can you believe that? They took me off all the safety-sensitive work, like I was some kind of liability, just because I was being thorough! They stuck me on sweeping duty and breaking down cardboard for like two weeks. It was humiliating, especially when I was the one working harder than anyone else in that whole warehouse. 

And then at home... well, my husband, he gets really frustrated. He says when I get like that, when I'm up all night boxing and making lists and talking a mile a minute, he just can't rely on me. Which I think is unfair, because I'm getting so much done! I'm organizing the whole house, I'm doing the church stuff, I'm working extra shifts. But he says I'm so scattered and so intense that he can't even have a normal conversation with me, let alone trust me to handle regular household stuff without turning it into some massive project. He told me last time that he feels like he's just watching a tornado tear through the house and he's just waiting for it to stop. So, yeah, I guess it does cause problems, even if I don't always agree with why people are upset about it. It just feels like nobody can keep up with me, and then they get mad at me for it.

Six months? Oh, it's been longer than that. Yeah, definitely longer. I'd say... well, it's been about eight months now. Eight whole months of dealing with this. I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time the weather started getting really cold, like late October, early November maybe? I was out in the garage, trying to fix the latch on the side door because the wind kept blowing it open, and that's the first time I heard him. Just this low, steady voice, right over my shoulder, telling me I was doing it wrong. I whipped around, and of course, nobody was there. Just me and the rakes. And ever since then, he just... he doesn't leave. Sometimes he's quiet for a bit, but he always comes back.

And the stuff at work, the sabotaging... that started right around the same time. Eight months of walking into the warehouse and just knowing, absolutely knowing, that they were messing with my pallets. I'd leave a stack perfectly shrink-wrapped, perfectly aligned, and I'd come back from my fifteen-minute break, and it would be slightly off. Just a fraction of an inch, but I could tell. I have an eye for that kind of thing. And they'd look at me, the shift manager and the other guys, they'd look at me with these little smirks, pretending they didn't do anything. But I know they did. They were moving things, changing the manifests, trying to make me look crazy or incompetent so I wouldn't get that supervisor job. So yeah, the voice, the feeling of being watched, the pallets being messed with... it's been a solid eight months of this, every single day, just wearing me down. It's exhausting, honestly, having to be on guard for eight straight months like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms have persisted for at least one month in the absence of mood symptoms, which best distinguishes schizophrenia from schizoaffective disorder and bipolar I disorder with psychotic features.
doctor.question: Have there been at least four straight weeks when you were hearing the man's voice or felt sure people were sabotaging you while your mood was completely normal?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: Even during a quieter few weeks when I was sleeping closer to normal and not racing around as much, I still heard the voice telling me to check things and believed the pallet counts were being changed against me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (hearing voices, feeling sabotaged) occurred during a period of normal mood for at least 4 straight weeks, which directly maps to the requirement of delusions and hallucinations occurring for 2 or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, there was a stretch exactly like that. Let me think... it was maybe a couple of months ago? I remember it clearly because my husband even made a comment about it. He was like, "Wow, it's nice you're actually sitting down to watch a movie with me," because usually, like I said, I'm up and down, pacing, fixing the weather stripping, making lists. But for like a solid month, maybe even five weeks, I was just... regular. I was having a really quiet few weeks. I was sleeping a good seven or eight hours a night, which is a huge deal for me, and I wasn't racing around trying to run the whole warehouse or signing up for a million church things. I was just clocking in, doing my job, coming home, eating dinner. Just a totally normal routine. 

But the thing is, even though I was feeling totally fine and my mood was completely calm, that guy's voice did not stop. Not even for a day. I’d be sitting there on the couch, drinking a soda, completely relaxed, and he’d be right there muttering at me, telling me I needed to go check things. Check the locks, check the garage, check my pallet stacks. It was constant. 

And the sabotage at work didn't stop either. I'd go in, feeling totally level, not fired up or arguing with anyone, but I still absolutely knew they were messing with my numbers. I'd look at the manifest and I could see that the pallet counts were being changed against me. Like, I’d wrap 42 pallets of freight, I'd count them twice, and then the shift sheet would suddenly say 40. I knew it was them

doctor.intent: Determine whether manic symptoms have caused marked impairment or required hospitalization, which best separates bipolar I disorder with psychotic features from schizophrenia/schizoaffective-like presentations here.
doctor.question: During one of those fired-up periods, were you ever hospitalized because of it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I was ever hospitalized during a manic period, but my symptom profile does not mention hospitalization (only being taken off forklift duties and issues at home).

patient.answer:
Hospitalized? No, no, I've never been in the hospital for any of this. I mean, I know sometimes people get so worked up they end up in the ER or something, but that hasn't happened to me. Even when I was pushing so hard for that supervisor job, and going up to the front office every single day with my lists, and calling everyone I knew, I was still, you know, functioning. I was still going to work, I was still showing up at church, I was still doing all the things I signed up for. It's not like I crashed my car or stopped eating or anything that would make someone call an ambulance. 

I mean, my husband, he definitely gets annoyed with me when I'm like that. He'll tell me to sit down, tell me I'm wearing him out just watching me. He says I talk too fast and I don't let him get a word in edgewise. And I guess I do get pretty intense, like with the boxing in the garage, I was out there at 3 AM hitting the bag so hard I thought the chain was going to snap. But even then, I wasn't hurting myself or anyone else. I was just... full of energy, you know? Just overflowing with it. So, no, no hospitals. I've always managed to ride it out at home, even if it drives everyone around me a little crazy while it's happening. I just keep moving until it finally starts to fade out on its own.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable episodes caused marked impairment requiring psychotic symptoms during mania to judge bipolar I with psychotic features versus schizophrenia/schizoaffective-like presentation.
doctor.question: During those fired-up periods, did the voice or your beliefs about sabotage ever get noticeably stronger than usual?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: During the weeks I was barely sleeping and pushing extra shifts, boxing, and church work, I was also hearing that man's voice and feeling sure people at the warehouse were setting me up.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the psychotic symptoms (the voice and beliefs about sabotage) occurred during the manic episode (fired-up periods), which directly matches the concurrent occurrence of psychotic and manic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Oh, absolutely. It all kind of... feeds into each other, you know? Like, when I'm in one of those really high-gear phases, when I'm barely sleeping, maybe getting two, three hours a night if I'm lucky, and I'm pushing for all those extra shifts at the warehouse, plus the 3 AM boxing sessions in the garage, plus organizing the bake sale and the clothing drive for the church all at the exact same time... that's when everything else gets dialed up to an eleven, too. 

It's like my brain is moving a million miles an hour, and the voice... the man's voice gets louder, more insistent. He doesn't just mutter when I'm fired up like that; he practically shouts. He'll be telling me I'm missing things, that I need to work faster, that I need to check the manifests again, check them three times, four times. And the sabotage stuff... oh man. When I'm running on that kind of energy, I am just so hyper-aware of everything. Every single look the shift manager gives me, every time someone walks past my pallets, I just know, I am absolutely certain they are plotting against me. I can see the whole setup so clearly. I'll be flying around the warehouse on a forklift, trying to do the work of three people to prove I deserve that supervisor spot, and I'll just feel it in my bones that they're actively trying to trip me up, changing the numbers on the clipboard the second I turn my back. So yeah, when I'm all revved up and doing a hundred things at once, the voice and the feeling that I'm being set up are right there with me, running just as fast and just as hard as I am. It's like they feed off the energy, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the fired-up periods caused marked impairment in functioning, which would support a manic episode and help distinguish bipolar I disorder from schizoaffective disorder or schizophrenia.
doctor.question: During those fired-up periods, did your behavior ever cause serious problems at work, at home, or with other people?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My supervisors took me off forklift and other safety-sensitive work because my counts and routines were slowing the line down, and at home my husband says he cannot rely on me the way he used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the manic ('fired-up') periods caused serious problems at work, at home, or socially, which directly assesses functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, yeah, I guess you could say it caused some problems. I mean, at work, it definitely did. It's actually really frustrating to think about, to be honest. See, when I was trying so hard to get that supervisor spot, and I was just buzzing with all that energy, I was checking things constantly. I mean, I had to, right? Because of the voice telling me to check, and because I knew they were messing with my numbers. So I'd be on the forklift, and I'd stop to recount a pallet, or I'd go back over my whole manifest three or four times, just to be absolutely sure everything was perfect. But my supervisors... they didn't see it that way. They pulled me into the office, and they were like, "You're slowing down the line, you're holding up the trucks," all this stuff. And then they actually took me off the forklift entirely. Can you believe that? They took me off all the safety-sensitive work, like I was some kind of liability, just because I was being thorough! They stuck me on sweeping duty and breaking down cardboard for like two weeks. It was humiliating, especially when I was the one working harder than anyone else in that whole warehouse. 

And then at home... well, my husband, he gets really frustrated. He says when I get like that, when I'm up all night boxing and making lists and talking a mile a minute, he just can't rely on me. Which I think is unfair, because I'm getting so much done! I'm organizing the whole house, I'm doing the church stuff, I'm working extra shifts. But he says I'm so scattered and so intense that he can't even have a normal conversation with me, let alone trust me to handle regular household stuff without turning it into some massive project. He told me last time that he feels like he's just watching a tornado tear through the house and he's just waiting for it to stop. So, yeah, I guess it does cause problems, even if I don't always agree with why people are upset about it. It just feels like nobody can keep up with me, and then they get mad at me for it.

inference.note: Psychosis persists for weeks with euthymic mood, supporting schizoaffective over bipolar with psychotic features; manic symptoms also cause marked impairment. Narrowed F25 to manic type.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has persistent psychotic symptoms for about 8 months, including auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions, plus clear manic episodes with decreased need for sleep, increased energy, irritability, increased goal-directed activity, and functional impairment. Crucially, psychotic symptoms were present for at least 4 weeks during a period of normal mood, supporting schizoaffective disorder, manic type, over bipolar I disorder with psychotic symptoms. Schizophrenia was considered, but the interview documents prominent syndromal manic episodes occurring during the illness course.
